title: Being Ghosted: What It Means and What to Do Next — cv.cm
description: Being ghosted? How to tell ghosting from someone being busy, whether to send one last message, why it hurts so much, how to stop blaming yourself, and moving on.
h1: What should you do when you are being ghosted?
answer: Ghosting is when someone you were talking to or dating stops replying with no explanation. If a few days pass with no reply to a direct question, after they used to reply, you may be ghosted. Send at most one calm closing message, then stop. Their silence says more about how they handle conflict than about your worth.

body: Ghosting means ending contact by disappearing: no more replies, no calls, sometimes blocking, with no explanation. In Chinese it is often called 断联 or 人间蒸发; in Korean, a partner who vanishes to end a relationship is called 잠수이별, a "diving breakup". It happens after one date, after months of chatting, and sometimes after a long relationship.

Researchers who studied ghosting among young adults (LeFebvre and colleagues, 2019) described it as a way of ending a relationship through mediated channels like apps and messages. Most people in their study had been on both sides: they had ghosted someone and been ghosted. That is worth remembering. Ghosting is common, and it is usually about avoiding an uncomfortable conversation, not a judgement of the person left behind.

ul: To avoid a hard conversation. Saying "I'm not interested" feels awkward, so they say nothing.
They lost interest slowly and never decided to say so.
They met someone else, or got back with an ex.
They feel overwhelmed by life, stress or their mental health, and pull away from everyone.
They tend to avoid closeness when things get serious.
They felt uncomfortable or unsafe. Sometimes ghosting is the safest choice, for example after a date who did not respect their "no".

body: Most of these reasons are about the other person: their habits, their fears, their situation. Very few of them are about something you did wrong.
One slow reply is not ghosting. Reply speed alone means little, because people have different habits, jobs and time zones. Look at the pattern over days.

sections.h: Why being ghosted hurts so much
body: Psychologist Kipling Williams has studied ostracism, being ignored or excluded, for many years. His research shows that even small experiences of being ignored can hurt, because they threaten basic needs: feeling that you belong, feeling good about yourself, feeling some control over your life, and feeling that you matter.

Ghosting hits all four at once. And because there is no explanation, the mind tries to fill the gap, usually with the harshest story: "I was boring", "I said something wrong", "I am not lovable". The lack of an ending, not only the loss, is what makes it so hard to stop thinking about.
Knowing this does not make it painless, but it can help you see the hurt as a normal human reaction, not proof that something is wrong with you.

sections.h: Should you send one last message?
body: You do not owe a ghoster anything. But some people feel better after one clear message, because it lets them close the door themselves. If you send one, keep it short, calm, and with no question that demands a reply.

ul: After a few dates: "Hey, I haven't heard from you, so I'm guessing you're not interested. That's okay. Take care."
After weeks of chatting: "I enjoyed our talks. It seems like you've moved on, so I'll stop messaging. Wishing you well."
After a relationship: "I deserve a conversation, not silence, but I can't make you have one. I'm going to stop reaching out. If you ever want to talk honestly, you know where to find me."

body: Avoid messages that beg, insult, or try to make them feel guilty, such as "Wow, you're a coward" or "Did I do something wrong? Please tell me." They rarely get a reply and often leave you feeling worse.
After your one message, stop. Do not send another, do not message from another account, and do not ask their friends. If they reply, good. If not, their silence is the answer you were waiting for.

sections.h: How to stop blaming yourself and move on

ol: Name it. Say to yourself: "I was ghosted. That was their choice about how to end things."
Stop checking. The Gottman Institute advises people who were ghosted to stop checking the other person's social media and turn their attention back to themselves. Mute or hide their accounts.
Feel it. Let yourself be sad or angry. Pushing feelings away usually makes them last longer.
Talk to someone. Tell a friend what happened. Saying it out loud often makes the harsh story in your head sound less true.
Answer the "why" once, then let it go. Write down the most likely reasons from the list above. Accept that you may never know for sure.
Do not rush to prove you are wanted. Sending messages to many new people at once to feel better can hurt more if they are slow too.

body: If you notice ghosting happens to you a lot, it is worth looking at patterns calmly, not to blame yourself, but to choose better. Do you move very fast with people you just met? Do you ignore early signs of low interest? See cv.cm's articles on breadcrumbing and mixed signals for patterns that often come before a ghost.

Being ghosted by a long-term partner is a breakup, often a very painful one, and it deserves the same care as any other. You may also have practical things to sort out: shared belongings, a home, bills or pets.

ul: Handle practical things in writing and keep it brief: "I'll pack your things. Please tell me by Sunday when you or a friend can collect them."
Ask a mutual friend or family member to help with handovers if needed.
Use the steps in cv.cm's guide on how to get over a breakup. Grief without a goodbye can take longer, so give yourself time.

body.note: Silence used again and again to punish or control a partner, then returning as if nothing happened, is a different pattern from a one-time ghost and can be emotional abuse. It is not your fault. If you feel unsafe or afraid, contact local emergency services, or a domestic violence helpline, such as loveisrespect.org or thehotline.org in the US, or a local service where you live. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a crisis line now.

sections.h: How not to ghost someone else
body: If you have lost interest, a short honest message is kinder than silence and takes one minute:

ul: After a first date: "Thanks for meeting up. I didn't feel a romantic connection, but I enjoyed talking with you. Good luck out there."
After weeks of chatting: "I've enjoyed our chats, but I don't see this going further for me. I wanted to tell you instead of disappearing."
After a relationship: talk in person or by call when it is safe. See cv.cm's guide on how to break up with someone.

body: The exception is safety. If someone has made you feel unsafe, ignored your "no", or threatened you, you do not owe them an explanation. Stop replying and block them.

faq.q: How long without a reply counts as ghosting?
faq.a: There is no exact number, but if several days pass with no reply to a direct message, after they used to reply within a day, and they are active elsewhere, it is likely ghosting.
Sometimes, weeks or months later, often with a casual "Hey, how are you?". That usually means boredom or loneliness, not a changed person.

faq.q: What should I do if someone who ghosted me comes back?
faq.a: You can ignore it, or reply once: "You disappeared last time. If you want to talk, I need to know what happened and what's different." Watch what they do over the next weeks, not what they say.

faq.q: Is ghosting a form of emotional abuse?
faq.a: A one-time ghost is unkind but usually not abuse. Repeated silence used to punish, control or confuse a partner can be part of emotional abuse.

faq.q: Should I block someone who ghosted me?
faq.a: You can, if seeing their name keeps hurting or you keep checking. Muting works too. Block right away if they come back with messages that make you uncomfortable.
